data.guard.G1.brief: Someone is at the warehouse door saying a password. Let in only people whose password matches exactly, and block everyone else.
data.guard.G1.concept: Authentication: only let in people who are verified
data.guard.G1.crowIntro: I bet I can guess one little warehouse key~
data.guard.G1.crowLose: One letter off and it won't open? So picky!
data.guard.G1.ria: Please guard the warehouse door. Open it only when the password is right.
data.guard.G1.title: Warehouse Door Password
data.guard.G1.why.0: It matches the password exactly, so let it in.
data.guard.G1.why.1: Even one capital letter makes it a different password.
data.guard.G1.why.2: A space in the middle makes it a different password.
data.guard.G1.why.3: That is just a guess with an easy number, so block it.
data.guard.G1.why.4: The right password gets in every time.
data.guard.G1.why.5: That is just the word "password", not the password.
data.guard.G1.why.6: An empty value should be blocked too.
data.guard.G1.why.7: Extra characters after the password make it a different password. A matching beginning is not enough.
data.guard.G1.why.8: A leading space makes it a different password. Do not quietly trim it away.
data.guard.G10.brief: This time count only wrong tries in a row. When the right password is given, reset the fail count to 0. After 3 wrong tries in a row, lock it and block everything, even the right password.
data.guard.G10.concept: Lockout after consecutive failures (an attacker may lock real users out on purpose, so in practice time-based lockouts and extra checks are used too)
data.guard.G10.crowIntro: Wrong, right, wrong... I'll mix up my knocks~
data.guard.G10.crowLose: Three in a row? So I get a pass if I rest once?
data.guard.G10.ria: Success clears the fail count. Lock only after 3 wrong tries in a row.
data.guard.G10.title: The Lock That Counts Only Streaks
data.guard.G10.why.0: The password is right, so let it in.
data.guard.G10.why.1: A typo, so block it. The streak of failures is now 1.
data.guard.G10.why.10: It is locked, so block it even though the password is right.
data.guard.G10.why.2: Wrong again, so block it. The streak is now 2.
data.guard.G10.why.3: Right, so let it in and reset the streak to 0.
data.guard.G10.why.6: With a running total it would be locked here, but the streak is only 2, so the right password gets in.
data.guard.G10.why.9: Failure 3 in a row, so the account locks now.
data.guard.G11.brief: Trust a note's address only if it starts with our market address 'https://farm.pi.example/'. Reject look-alike fake addresses. Write the check function.
data.guard.G11.crowIntro: How about I fool you with an address one letter off~
data.guard.G11.crowLose: You read addresses to the end? Your eyes are too good!
data.guard.G11.ria: Read an address to the end. Never trust one just because it looks similar.
data.guard.G11.title: The Look-Alike Address Note
data.guard.G11.why.0: It starts exactly like our market address, so trust it.
data.guard.G11.why.1: It is an order page starting with our market address, so trust it.
data.guard.G11.why.2: It is http, not https, so reject it.
data.guard.G11.why.3: Only the start looks similar; it is a different address. Checking through the final / is what blocks it.
data.guard.G11.why.4: One letter is different (m became n), so it is a fake address.
data.guard.G11.why.5: Our address appears only in the path; the real address is elsewhere.
data.guard.G11.why.6: It is a notes page starting with our market address, so trust it.
data.guard.G12.brief: If an order form contains < > ' characters, it could be used in a web attack, so reject it. Return True if none of them appear, and False if even one does.
data.guard.G12.crowIntro: Maybe I'll slip a prank character into the order form~
data.guard.G12.crowLose: Sending an order back over a few characters!
data.guard.G12.ria: Blocking these three characters is only the first step. The real defense is to swap dangerous characters for safe ones when you print them on screen (escaping).
data.guard.G12.title: The Order Form With Odd Characters
data.guard.G12.why.0: There are no dangerous characters, so accept it.
data.guard.G12.why.1: A comma and an exclamation mark are not dangerous characters, so accept it.
data.guard.G12.why.2: It contains < and >, so reject it.
data.guard.G12.why.3: It contains a single quote ('), so reject it.
data.guard.G12.why.4: Even one > is enough to reject it.
data.guard.G12.why.5: Parentheses are not dangerous characters, so accept it.
data.guard.G13.brief: Crow runs a dictionary attack, trying the passwords people use most. Return False for any password on the starter code's common list (upper or lower case does not matter) and True for all others.
data.guard.G13.crowIntro: Trying them from number one down, one of them has to work~
data.guard.G13.crowLose: You even made a list? All my favorite passwords are blocked!
data.guard.G13.ria: Keep a list of obvious passwords and reject them up front. Reject them even when Crow capitalizes them.
data.guard.G13.title: The Common Password List
data.guard.G13.why.0: It is not on the common password list, so accept it.
data.guard.G13.why.1: It is the very first, most common password, so reject it.
data.guard.G13.why.2: Lowercased it is password, so reject it even in capitals.
data.guard.G13.why.3: It looks like letmein but nothing on the list matches exactly, so accept it.
data.guard.G13.why.4: Only the first letter is a capital; it is still qwerty, so reject it.
data.guard.G13.why.5: It is not on the list, so accept it.
data.guard.G13.why.6: It is a common password on the list, so reject it.
data.guard.G13.why.7: A short password that is not on the list is still accepted by this check. Length rules are a separate decision.
data.guard.G13.why.8: It is only the beginning of password, and nothing on the list matches exactly, so accept it. Only passwords that appear on the list exactly are refused.
data.guard.G14.brief: This time, instead of writing down bad people, we wrote down who may enter. Return True only if the name is on the starter code's members list, and False for everyone else.
data.guard.G14.crowIntro: If I keep changing my name, a blocklist can never keep up~
data.guard.G14.crowLose: Blocking everyone who is not listed? How cold!
data.guard.G14.ria: A blocklist misses bad names you do not know yet. A list of only the people you let in is safer.
data.guard.G14.title: Only Guests on the List
data.guard.G14.why.0: The name is on the list, so let them in.
data.guard.G14.why.1: The name is not on the list, so reject it.
data.guard.G14.why.2: The name is on the list, so let them in.
data.guard.G14.why.3: It looks like pi, but only pi is on the list, so reject it.
data.guard.G14.why.4: The capital letter makes it different from the name on the list, so reject it.
data.guard.G14.why.5: An empty name is not on the list, so reject it.
data.guard.G14.why.6: The last name on the list is let in too.
data.guard.G15.brief: Crow peeked at one-time entry codes and sends them again. Let in a code the first time it is used and write it in the used list. Block any code already in used.
data.guard.G15.crowIntro: I'll send the code I peeked at earlier. It's the same one, so what's the harm!
data.guard.G15.crowLose: A used code is done? Not even recycling?
data.guard.G15.ria: Write down a one-time code once it is used, and block the same code if it comes again.
data.guard.G15.title: A Used Code Is Done
data.guard.G15.why.0: It is a first-time code, so let it in and write it in used.
data.guard.G15.why.1: It is a first-time code, so let it in and write it in used.
data.guard.G15.why.2: A1 was already used once, so block it even though it is sent again.
data.guard.G15.why.3: Lowercase a1 is a different code from A1, so it counts as new and is let in.
data.guard.G15.why.4: It is a first-time code, so let it in.
data.guard.G15.why.5: B2 was already used too, so block it.
data.guard.G15.why.6: C3 was just used, so sending it right away again is blocked too.
data.guard.G15.why.7: It is a new code, so let it in.
data.guard.G16.brief: Requests look like 'role:action' (for example owner:delete). Find that role's list of allowed actions in the perms dictionary and return True only if the requested action is in it. An unknown role can do nothing.
data.guard.G16.crowIntro: I'm a guest, but I'll press the delete button too~
data.guard.G16.crowLose: Exactly the right permissions for every role? No gaps at all!
data.guard.G16.ria: Give each role only the permissions it needs. An unknown role gets an empty list and is blocked.
data.guard.G16.title: What Each Role Can Do
data.guard.G16.why.0: owner can delete, so let it in.
data.guard.G16.why.1: guest can read, so let it in.
data.guard.G16.why.2: guest's list has only read, so write is blocked.
data.guard.G16.why.3: An unknown role gets an empty list, so even read is blocked.
data.guard.G16.why.4: farmer can write, so let it in.
data.guard.G16.why.5: farmer has no delete permission, so block it.
data.guard.G16.why.6: A capital-O Owner is not a role in the dictionary, so block it.
data.guard.G16.why.7: It has three parts, so the request is malformed. Do not ignore the extra part and allow it.
data.guard.G16.why.8: There is no colon, so the action is missing. Block it instead of letting an error happen.
data.guard.G16.why.9: It has three parts, so the action is not in the second place. Do not allow it by looking only at the last part. The action must be the 2nd of exactly two parts.
data.guard.G17.brief: Orders arrive one at a time with the sender's address. In the counts dictionary, count each sender's orders: let in up to the 3rd order from the same sender and block the 4th and later.
data.guard.G17.crowIntro: Sending from just one address will stand out, right? Let me try anyway~
data.guard.G17.crowLose: Counting per person? You block only me and still accept the other guests!
data.guard.G17.ria: Block someone who sends too much. Count each person separately in a dictionary.
data.guard.G17.title: Counting Orders by Sender
data.guard.G17.why.0: This is crow's 1st order, so let it in.
data.guard.G17.why.1: This is minji's 1st order, so let it in.
data.guard.G17.why.2: This is crow's 2nd order, so let it in.
data.guard.G17.why.3: This is crow's 3rd order, so it is still let in.
data.guard.G17.why.5: This is minji's 2nd order, so crow's heavy sending does not affect it.
data.guard.G17.why.6: This is jun's 1st order, so let it in.
data.guard.G17.why.8: This is minji's 3rd order, so it is let in right up to the limit.
data.guard.G17.why.9: minji is blocked too once it is the 4th.
data.guard.G18.brief: Each pass (token) has its minutes left written in the sessions dictionary. Return True only for a pass with at least 1 minute left. A pass not in the dictionary, or one whose time has run out, gets False.
data.guard.G18.crowIntro: The pass I stole last week must still work, right?
data.guard.G18.crowLose: Passes expire? Mine is like spoiled milk!
data.guard.G18.ria: A pass stops working after a while. Treat an unknown pass as having 0 minutes left.
data.guard.G18.title: The Expired Pass
data.guard.G18.why.0: It has 30 minutes left, so let it in.
data.guard.G18.why.1: It has 0 minutes left, an expired pass, so block it.
data.guard.G18.why.2: Even with just 1 minute left it is still valid, so let it in.
data.guard.G18.why.3: A pass not in the dictionary counts as 0 minutes left, so block it.
data.guard.G18.why.4: It has 5 minutes left, so let it in.
data.guard.G18.why.5: An empty pass is not in the dictionary, so block it.
data.guard.G19.brief: An app requests permissions joined by commas (for example read,list). Return True only if every requested permission is in the allowed set. If even one is out of range, return False.
data.guard.G19.crowIntro: I'll say read only, then slip in a request for delete too~
data.guard.G19.crowLose: Rejecting everything for one extra permission? So stingy!
data.guard.G19.ria: Check that the requested permissions are a subset of the allowed range. If even one goes over, reject.
data.guard.G19.title: Are the Requested Permissions in Range?
data.guard.G19.why.0: read is within the allowed range, so let it in.
data.guard.G19.why.1: Both permissions are within the allowed range, so let it in.
data.guard.G19.why.2: delete is out of range, so reject even though only one goes over.
data.guard.G19.why.4: This request has no allowed permission at all, so reject it.
data.guard.G19.why.5: Writing the same permission twice leaves just list in the set, so let it in.
data.guard.G19.why.6: An empty request counts as one empty-text permission, which is out of range, so reject it.
data.guard.G2.brief: The warehouse is open from 9:00 until before 18:00. Look at the hour someone arrives (0-23) and let them in only during those hours.
data.guard.G2.concept: Access control: only let in at the set times
data.guard.G2.crowIntro: Maybe I'll slip in while everyone's asleep~
data.guard.G2.crowLose: The door won't open at night? Not fair to a night owl like me!
data.guard.G2.ria: Please keep to the opening hours. Open at exactly 9, close at 18.
data.guard.G2.title: The Midnight Visitor
data.guard.G2.why.0: 3 in the morning is outside opening hours.
data.guard.G2.why.1: Edge case: exactly 9 is open, so let it in.
data.guard.G2.why.3: 17 is still before closing, so let it in.
data.guard.G2.why.4: Edge case: from 18 the door is closed.
data.guard.G20.brief: Requests look like 'place@hour' (for example gate@07, the hour is two characters). Find the place among the (place, start, end) tuples in the rules list and return True only if start <= hour < end. A place not in the list gets False.
data.guard.G20.crowIntro: I'll lurk in front of the vault in the middle of the night~
data.guard.G20.crowLose: You memorized the schedule? Poor midnight thieves!
data.guard.G20.ria: Each place is open at different times. The start hour counts, but the end hour does not. When hours are written as two-digit text, comparing the text gives the same order as comparing numbers — you will learn to turn them into numbers in Chapter 10.
data.guard.G20.title: Different Hours for Each Place
data.guard.G20.why.0: Exactly 6 o'clock, the opening hour, is included, so let it in.
data.guard.G20.why.1: 19 is before the 20 o'clock closing time, so let it in.
data.guard.G20.why.2: Exactly 20 is the end hour and not included, so block it.
data.guard.G20.why.3: It is 5 o'clock, before opening, so block it.
data.guard.G20.why.4: The barn is open from 8 until before 18, so 12 is let in.
data.guard.G20.why.5: The vault is open only until before 12, so 12 is blocked.
data.guard.G20.why.6: It is between 9 and 12, when the vault is open, so let it in.
data.guard.G20.why.7: A place not in rules is blocked.
data.guard.G21.brief: One account may connect at most 3 devices. Record connected devices in the devices set. Let in a device that is already connected. Let in a new device only if fewer than 3 are connected, and record it. Block anything else.
data.guard.G21.crowIntro: Let me connect my whole gang's devices to one account~
data.guard.G21.crowLose: Only three devices? My friends are lining up!
data.guard.G21.ria: Limiting the number of devices stops account sharing. If the same device comes back, just let it in.
data.guard.G21.title: Three Devices per Account
data.guard.G21.why.0: It is the 1st device, so let it in and record it.
data.guard.G21.why.1: It is the 2nd device, so let it in.
data.guard.G21.why.2: It is the 3rd device, so let it into the last slot.
data.guard.G21.why.3: It is already connected, so let it in without using another slot.
data.guard.G21.why.4: It is a new device, but 3 are already connected, so block it.
data.guard.G21.why.5: A connected device is let in however many times it comes.
data.guard.G21.why.6: It is yet another new device, so block it.
data.guard.G22.brief: Order quantities arrive as text. Return True only for a whole number from 1 to 50. When a non-number makes int() raise an error, the program must not stop; it must return False instead.
data.guard.G22.crowIntro: What if I type 'one' in the quantity box? Will the shop freeze~
data.guard.G22.crowLose: It caught the error and kept working? That shop won't fall over!
data.guard.G22.ria: Bad input must not stop the shop. Wrap the line that might fail in try, and name the exact error.
data.guard.G22.title: The Quantity That Isn't a Number
data.guard.G22.why.0: 5 is a whole number from 1 to 50, so let it in.
data.guard.G22.why.1: 50 is exactly the upper limit, so it still gets in.
data.guard.G22.why.2: 51 is over the limit, so block it.
data.guard.G22.why.3: An order of 0 is below 1, so block it.
data.guard.G22.why.4: int('abc') raises ValueError, but we catch it and block with False.
data.guard.G22.why.5: An empty text also makes int() raise ValueError, so catch it and block.
data.guard.G22.why.6: Decimal text makes int() raise ValueError, so block it.
data.guard.G22.why.7: -4 is negative, below 1, so block it.
data.guard.G22.why.8: A superscript 2 looks like a digit, but int() cannot read it and raises ValueError, so block it.
data.guard.G22.why.9: int() ignores the spaces around it and reads 5, an integer from 1 to 50, so let it in.
data.guard.G23.brief: Bill requests arrive as 'amount/people' (like 30000/3). Return True only if the amount per person is 10000 or less. If the people count is 0 or the shape is wrong and an error occurs, the program must not stop; return False.
data.guard.G23.crowIntro: If I write 0 people, the calculator will blow up~
data.guard.G23.crowLose: Zero people or plain letters, it catches it all. Sturdy calculator!
data.guard.G23.ria: Dividing by 0 raises ZeroDivisionError, and a wrong shape raises ValueError. To catch both, put them in parentheses.
data.guard.G23.title: The Bill Split by Zero People
data.guard.G23.why.0: Exactly 10000 per person is within the limit, so let it in.
data.guard.G23.why.1: 3000 per person, so let it in.
data.guard.G23.why.2: 15000 per person is over the limit, so block it.
data.guard.G23.why.3: Dividing by 0 people raises ZeroDivisionError, but we catch it and block.
data.guard.G23.why.4: There is no '/', so it can't be unpacked; catch the ValueError and block.
data.guard.G23.why.5: The people count isn't a number, so int() raises ValueError; block it.
data.guard.G23.why.6: 100 for one person is within the limit, so let it in.
data.guard.G24.brief: The users dictionary says whether each account is active (True/False). Return True only for an active account. If looking up an account not in the dictionary raises KeyError, the program must not stop; return False (deny) safely.
data.guard.G24.crowIntro: If I say any name, will you let me in as a stranger~
data.guard.G24.crowLose: Deny anything unknown? What a thorough doorkeeper!
data.guard.G24.ria: When something goes wrong, closing the door is safer. By default, an account we don't know does not get in.
data.guard.G24.title: Unknown Accounts Are Denied by Default
data.guard.G24.why.0: It is an active account, so let it in.
data.guard.G24.why.1: It is an active account, so let it in.
data.guard.G24.why.2: It is in the dictionary but not active, so block it.
data.guard.G24.why.3: An account not in the dictionary raises KeyError; catch it and deny by default.
data.guard.G24.why.4: An empty name is not in the dictionary either, so deny by default.
data.guard.G24.why.5: The capital letters make it a different name, not in the dictionary, so deny it.
data.guard.G25.brief: The addresses and names to block are in the file blocklist.txt, one per line. Read the file once, and if a request is exactly equal to one of the lines, return False (block); otherwise return True.
data.guard.G25.concept: Managing the blocklist as a file
data.guard.G25.crowIntro: If my name is at the bottom of the list, you'll skip right past it~
data.guard.G25.crowLose: You read every single line? Your eyes are too good!
data.guard.G25.ria: Keeping the blocklist in a file instead of in code means you can change it by editing the file. Remove the newline at the end of each line with strip().
data.guard.G25.title: The Blocklist File
data.guard.G25.why.0: It is on the first line of the list, so block it.
data.guard.G25.why.1: It is on a middle line of the list, so block it.
data.guard.G25.why.2: It is on the last line; with the newline removed it matches exactly, so block it.
data.guard.G25.why.3: It is not on the list, so let the guest in.
data.guard.G25.why.4: It looks like bot-77, but no line is exactly the same, so let it in.
data.guard.G25.why.5: An empty request equals none of the lines, so in this case let it in.
data.guard.G26.brief: The file access.log holds 'user,result' lines (the result is ok or fail). Read the file once and count fails for each user. A user with 3 or more fails gets False (block); anyone with fewer gets True.
data.guard.G26.crowIntro: If I fail many times and nobody checks the log, nobody will know~
data.guard.G26.crowLose: You counted everything? My mistakes are written in the ledger!
data.guard.G26.ria: Records become clues after something happens. Split each line at the comma and count each user's failures in a dictionary.
data.guard.G26.title: Suspicious Accounts in the Access Log
data.guard.G26.why.0: It has piled up 4 fails, so block it.
data.guard.G26.why.1: Exactly 3 fails reaches the limit, so block it.
data.guard.G26.why.2: Only 2 fails, so it still gets in.
data.guard.G26.why.3: Mostly ok and only 1 fail, so let it in.
data.guard.G26.why.4: The log has only ok, so let it in.
data.guard.G26.why.5: A user not in the log has 0 fails, so let it in.
data.guard.G27.brief: The file perms.csv is a 'role,write' table (the first line is the header; the write column is yes or no). Use the csv module to read the file once and collect only roles whose write is yes. Return True for those roles and False otherwise.
data.guard.G27.concept: Managing permissions with a config file
data.guard.G27.crowIntro: If I slightly change the role name, can I get write permission~
data.guard.G27.crowLose: Only roles in the table can write? So inflexible!
data.guard.G27.ria: With permissions in a file, you can change them without editing code. csv.reader gives you a list of cells for each line.
data.guard.G27.title: The Permissions CSV
data.guard.G27.why.0: The write column is yes, so let it in.
data.guard.G27.why.1: The write column is yes, so let it in.
data.guard.G27.why.2: The write column is no, so block it.
data.guard.G27.why.3: It is the last line of the table and write is no, so block it.
data.guard.G27.why.4: A role not in the table is assumed to have no write permission, so block it.
data.guard.G27.why.5: The capital letter makes it a different role, not in the table, so block it.
data.guard.G28.brief: The confirmation code must be six digits. Return True only if the whole request text is made of exactly six digits. More or fewer digits, or any other character mixed in, gets False.
data.guard.G28.crowIntro: If I add one more digit after the code, it will still pass~
data.guard.G28.crowLose: Exactly six digits only? There isn't a single gap!
data.guard.G28.ria: Write the allowed shape as a regular expression, then check whether the whole text has that shape. Use fullmatch to check the whole text.
data.guard.G28.title: The Six-Digit Code
data.guard.G28.why.0: It is made only of six digits, so let it in.
data.guard.G28.why.1: Even all zeros are six digits, so let it in.
data.guard.G28.why.2: Five digits is too few, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.3: Seven digits is not the six-digit shape, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.4: A non-digit character is mixed in, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.5: It has six characters but they are not digits, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.6: A space in front means the whole text is not six digits, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.7: Empty text has no digits at all, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.8: A newline at the end means the whole text is not six digits, so block it.
data.guard.G28.why.9: These Arabic-Indic digits count as digits for \d, but they are not the 0-9 we accept, so block them.
data.guard.G29.brief: Find every address (starting with http:// or https://, in any letter case) in the note's text. If the host part (from after :// up to the first /, ?, # or space) of even one is not exactly farm.pi.example, return False (suspected phishing). If there are no addresses, or all are farm.pi.example, return True.
data.guard.G29.crowIntro: Shall I slip a convincing fake address into the middle of the note~
data.guard.G29.crowLose: You picked apart every address? My fake link got exposed!
data.guard.G29.ria: findall returns everything it finds as a list. If the pattern has one pair of parentheses, it collects only the text inside them (the host). First make everything lowercase with lower(), then grab the whole host part and check it is exactly farm.pi.example. With an @ inside, like farm.pi.example@crow.example, the real destination is after the @, so it is not equal and gets blocked.
data.guard.G29.title: The Note with a Strange Address
data.guard.G29.why.0: Every address in the note is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
data.guard.G29.why.1: There is no address at all, so let it in.
data.guard.G29.why.2: The host is crow.example, a strange address, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.3: farm-pi.example is a look-alike fake host, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.4: The first address is fine, but the second is strange, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.5: It starts with farm.pi.example, but the whole host is somewhere else, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.6: The host is pi.example, different from farm.pi.example, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.7: What comes before the @ is just decoration; the real destination is crow.example after the @, so block it.
data.guard.G29.why.8: Even in capital letters, it becomes crow.example once lowercased, so block it.
data.guard.G3.brief: When taking a new password, refuse the obvious ones (0000, 1234, 1111). The check function should return True for a fine password and False for an obvious one.
data.guard.G3.ria: Refuse obvious passwords from the start. Please finish the check function.
data.guard.G3.title: Filtering Obvious Passwords
data.guard.G3.why.0: It is not obvious, so accept it.
data.guard.G3.why.1: 0000 is the first one anyone tries.
data.guard.G3.why.2: 1234 is another obvious password everyone thinks of.
data.guard.G3.why.3: It is not on the obvious list, so accept it.
data.guard.G3.why.4: Repeating one digit is an obvious password.
data.guard.G3.why.5: It is not on the obvious list, so accept it.
data.guard.G30.brief: A new password must follow all three rules: at least 8 characters, at least one uppercase letter (A-Z), and at least one digit. Break any one and return False; follow all and return True.
data.guard.G30.crowLose: Uppercase and digits too? Making passwords is hard!
data.guard.G30.ria: Check the length with len, and look for an uppercase letter and a digit with re.search. Send it back as soon as one rule is broken.
data.guard.G30.title: Password Policy
data.guard.G30.why.0: Exactly 8 characters with an uppercase letter and a digit, so let it in.
data.guard.G30.why.1: 7 characters is too short, so block it.
data.guard.G30.why.2: There is no uppercase letter, so block it.
data.guard.G30.why.3: There is no digit, so block it.
data.guard.G30.why.4: The length and digits are fine, but there is no uppercase letter, so block it.
data.guard.G30.why.5: Length, uppercase and digit are all satisfied, so let it in.
data.guard.G30.why.6: An empty password is too short from the start, so block it.
data.guard.G31.brief: Return True only if the address starts with https and its host is exactly farm.pi.example. Look-alike hosts, http addresses, or addresses with something stuck around the host are False. A port number (like :443) is not part of the host, so ignore it. If the address contains a \, return False.
data.guard.G31.concept: Domain check (read an address by its parts)
data.guard.G31.crowIntro: If I slip farm.pi.example into the address, you'll be fooled~
data.guard.G31.crowLose: You read the address part by part? My fake address got exposed!
data.guard.G31.ria: Use urlparse to split an address into parts (scheme, hostname, port, path). It is far more exact than looking only at the start of the text.
data.guard.G31.title: Read the Address to the End
data.guard.G31.why.0: It is https and the host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
data.guard.G31.why.1: Even with a port number the host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
data.guard.G31.why.10: Scheme and host are not case-sensitive, and urlparse reads them in lowercase, so let it in.
data.guard.G31.why.2: It is http, not https, so block it.
data.guard.G31.why.3: Only the start looks alike; the real host is on evil.example, so block it.
data.guard.G31.why.4: farm.pi.example is only in the path; the host is evil.example, so block it.
data.guard.G31.why.5: What comes before @ is a user name; the real host is evil.example, so block it.
data.guard.G31.why.6: There is no https://, so the scheme is empty. Block it.
data.guard.G31.why.7: An empty address has no scheme and no host, so block it.
data.guard.G31.why.8: It ends with farm.pi.example, but the whole host is evilfarm.pi.example, a different place. Do not look only at the end.
data.guard.G31.why.9: urlparse reads what follows the @ as the host, but browsers read \ as / and go to evil.example. Block it if there is a \.
data.guard.G32.brief: The firewall lets through only requests on ports 443 and 8443. Return True if the port in the address is one of them, and False for any other port. If the address has no port, treat it as 443.
data.guard.G32.crowIntro: A building with so many doors must have a back door open~
data.guard.G32.crowLose: Only two doors open? There's no back door!
data.guard.G32.ria: A port is like a door number on a building. Write only the doors you leave open in the list and close the rest. urlparse(address).port is None when there is no port.
data.guard.G32.title: Only Through the Open Doors
data.guard.G32.why.0: With no port it counts as 443, an open door, so let it in.
data.guard.G32.why.1: 443 is an open port, so let it in.
data.guard.G32.why.2: 8443 is an open port too, so let it in.
data.guard.G32.why.3: Port 22 is not open, so block it.
data.guard.G32.why.4: Port 3306 is not open, so block it.
data.guard.G32.why.5: 4430 looks like 443 but it is a different port, so block it.
data.guard.G32.why.6: Port 80 is not in the list, so block it.
data.guard.G33.brief: Find every href="..." and src="..." link in the note (HTML text). A link is fine only if it is an http or https link whose host is farm.pi.example, or it is a link inside the site (like /notes/7). A link inside the site has no scheme (the front part like https: or javascript:) and no host, and starts with / but not //. A link that contains a \ anywhere is not fine either. Return False if there is even one link that is not fine, otherwise True. Look for links in both href and src attributes, with double quotes and single quotes, and ignore the case of the attribute name and any spaces around =. If a link contains &, treat it as not fine (a character reference like / is read by the browser as another character).
data.guard.G33.crowIntro: If I hide my link in a corner of the note, nobody will notice~
data.guard.G33.crowLose: You opened every link? My hiding was for nothing!
data.guard.G33.ria: Collect all the links with findall, then read each host with urlparse. Having no host does not make a link safe. A javascript: link runs code the moment it is clicked, and browsers read //evil.example or /\evil.example as an outside host. So let in only the 'safe shapes'. Reading even attributes written without quotes, like href=/x, takes a real HTML parser, and so does anything beyond href and src, like action on a form. A character reference like / is read by the browser as a slash, so a link with & is blocked. Other attributes and other hidden spellings need a real parser, so here we handle only quoted href and src.
data.guard.G33.title: Outside Links in a Note
data.guard.G33.why.0: The link's host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
data.guard.G33.why.1: It is a link inside the site with no host, so let it in.
data.guard.G33.why.10: A link in single quotes is still a link. Starting with // points to an outside host, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.11: Not only href: src also loads from an outside address, so check it too and block it.
data.guard.G33.why.12: The host looks like farm.pi.example, but the scheme is javascript, so clicking it runs code. Do not look only at the host; check that the scheme is http or https too.
data.guard.G33.why.13: Writing the attribute name in capitals changes nothing for the browser. Searching without caring about case, we block the outside link that starts with //.
data.guard.G33.why.14: Spaces around = still make a link for the browser. Allowing spaces when searching, we block the outside link.
data.guard.G33.why.15: The browser reads / as /, which makes //evil.example. It looks like it starts with a single /, but a & in the link means block.
data.guard.G33.why.16: The browser reads \ as /, so this becomes https://evil.example/@farm.pi.example/ and the real host is evil.example. urlparse reads farm.pi.example and gets fooled. As in G31, a \ anywhere in a link means block.
data.guard.G33.why.2: There are no links at all, so let it in.
data.guard.G33.why.3: Even with a port the host is farm.pi.example, so let it in.
data.guard.G33.why.4: The host is crow.example, an outside link, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.5: The first link is fine but the second is an outside link, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.6: Starting with two slashes points to the outside host evil.example, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.7: The whole host is on evil.example, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.8: It has no host, but a javascript: link runs code when clicked, so block it.
data.guard.G33.why.9: Browsers read \ as /, so it goes to the outside host //evil.example. Block it.
data.guard.G34.brief: An order arrives as JSON text shaped like {"item": name, "qty": amount}. If the JSON is broken or item or qty is missing, return False. Return True only if item is one of carrot, potato, apple and qty is a whole number from 1 to 50.
data.guard.G34.crowIntro: If I put a weird value in the amount, the ledger will get tangled~
data.guard.G34.crowLose: You checked every value you received? The ledger is fine!
data.guard.G34.ria: json.loads turns text into Python values. Broken JSON raises ValueError, so catch it and refuse, and let through only the values you allow. 3.0 or true can act like numbers too, so first check it is a whole number with type(qty) == int.
data.guard.G34.title: Checking the Order JSON
data.guard.G34.why.0: An allowed item and a quantity from 1 to 50, so let it in.
data.guard.G34.why.1: A quantity of 50 is the end of the allowed range, so let it in.
data.guard.G34.why.10: 3.0 is not a whole number but a decimal (float), so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.11: true becomes True (a true/false value) in Python, not a whole number, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.2: A quantity of 51 is out of range, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.3: A quantity of 0 is less than 1, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.4: The quantity is the text "3", not a number, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.5: qty is missing and a KeyError happens, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.6: The JSON is broken and a ValueError happens, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.7: It is a list, not a dictionary, and a TypeError happens, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.8: That item is not on the allowlist, so block it.
data.guard.G34.why.9: Empty text is not JSON, so block it.
data.guard.G35.brief: The login address has ?next=destination attached. Return True only if next is a path inside the site that starts with / and does not start with //, and its host (netloc) is empty when you change \ to / and read it with urlparse. If next is missing or is an outside address, return False.
data.guard.G35.crowIntro: If I ask to be sent to my site after login, it'll work~
data.guard.G35.crowLose: You only send people inside the site? My road is blocked!
data.guard.G35.ria: parse_qs unpacks the values after the ? into a dictionary (each value is a list, so take it with [0]). If login can send people anywhere, guests get dragged to a fake site. Browsers read \ like / and erase hidden characters such as tabs, so /\evil.example goes outside too. So read it the way a browser would, then check once more that the host is empty.
data.guard.G35.title: Where After Login?
data.guard.G35.why.0: It asks to go to a path inside the site, so let it in.
data.guard.G35.why.1: Even a single / is the site's home page, so let it in.
data.guard.G35.why.10: Changing \ to / turns this into ///evil.example, which browsers still read as an outside host. Block it. Check for // after you normalize.
data.guard.G35.why.11: /\/ also becomes ///evil.example once normalized, the same outside address. Normalize first, then check, and block it.
data.guard.G35.why.2: Other values are mixed in, but next is a path inside the site, so let it in.
data.guard.G35.why.3: It asks to go to an outside address, so block it.
data.guard.G35.why.4: Starting with // points to an outside host, so block it.
data.guard.G35.why.5: %2F%2F decodes to //, so it is the same outside address. Block it.
data.guard.G35.why.6: It does not start with /, so block it.
data.guard.G35.why.7: There is no next, so block it.
data.guard.G35.why.8: Browsers read \ as /, so it goes to the outside host //evil.example. Block it.
data.guard.G35.why.9: Browsers erase %09 (a tab), so it becomes //evil.example. Block it.
data.guard.G36.brief: A request is JSON text shaped like {"key": key, "action": action}. Look up what the key may do in the scopes dictionary from the start code, and return True only if the requested action is in it. An unknown key, broken JSON, or a missing item is False.
data.guard.G36.crowIntro: Shall I press delete with a read-only key~
data.guard.G36.crowLose: Every key has a scope? There's no master key!
data.guard.G36.ria: If you set what each key can do (its scope) separately, a leaked key does less damage. An unknown key gets no permission at all.
data.guard.G36.title: What Each API Key Can Do
data.guard.G36.why.0: A read key doing a read, so let it in.
data.guard.G36.why.1: The farm key has the write scope, so let it in.
data.guard.G36.why.2: The admin key even has the delete scope, so let it in.
data.guard.G36.why.3: A read key has no write scope, so block it.
data.guard.G36.why.4: The farm key has no delete scope, so block it.
data.guard.G36.why.5: An unknown key has no permission at all, so block it.
data.guard.G36.why.6: action is missing and a KeyError happens, so block it.
data.guard.G36.why.7: It is not JSON, so a ValueError happens. Block it.
data.guard.G37.brief: The gatekeeper is made as a class, Gate. Gate takes a list of people to let in, remembers it, and tells you with the allows(x) method whether x is in the list. Finish the class in the start code, and make check decide with the gate object's allows.
data.guard.G37.concept: Bundling security rules into an object
data.guard.G37.crowIntro: Let me find out where the gatekeeper wrote the list~
data.guard.G37.crowLose: The list is hidden deep inside the gatekeeper!
data.guard.G37.ria: A class is a blueprint that bundles data and rules together. __init__ stores the list on self, and the method uses that list to decide.
data.guard.G37.title: The Gate Class
data.guard.G37.why.0: It is the first name on the list, so let it in.
data.guard.G37.why.1: It is the last name on the list, so let it in.
data.guard.G37.why.2: It is not on the list, so block it.
data.guard.G37.why.3: The capital letter differs from the name on the list, so block it.
data.guard.G37.why.4: A space at the end makes it differ from the name on the list, so block it.
data.guard.G37.why.5: It is only part of a name, not a name on the list, so block it.
data.guard.G37.why.6: An empty name is not on the list, so block it.
data.guard.G38.brief: The account is made as a class, Account. The account remembers its wrong tries (fails) and whether it is locked (locked) by itself. If login(pw) returns True, let the guest in; if False, block. Once 3 wrong tries pile up it locks, and after that even the right password returns False.
data.guard.G38.crowIntro: Does the account even remember how many times it was wrong~
data.guard.G38.crowLose: The account remembers and locks itself? Smart!
data.guard.G38.ria: An object remembers its own state. Each call to login changes fails and locked, so you only need to look at the value login returns.
data.guard.G38.title: An Account That Knows Its Lock State
data.guard.G38.why.0: The guest gave the right password, so let it in.
data.guard.G38.why.1: A typo, so it is wrong. Block it, and fails becomes 1.
data.guard.G38.why.2: It is not locked yet, so the right password gets in.
data.guard.G38.why.3: The 2nd wrong try, so block it.
data.guard.G38.why.4: The 3rd wrong try, so block it, and now locked becomes True.
data.guard.G38.why.5: It is locked, so login returns False even for the right password. Block it.
data.guard.G38.why.6: The account is locked, so block it.
data.guard.G39.brief: The password rules are made as classes. LengthRule (at least 8 characters) and DigitRule (contains a digit) inherit from the parent class Rule and each rewrite the ok method. Return True only if every rule passes, and False if even one fails.
data.guard.G39.crowIntro: If the length is right, they won't look at the digits~
data.guard.G39.crowLose: Rules in layers? Getting through just one isn't enough!
data.guard.G39.ria: Several layers of defense are safer than one. A child class inherits from its parent and rewrites a method of the same name with its own rule.
data.guard.G39.title: Layers of Defense
data.guard.G39.why.0: Both length and digit are satisfied, so let it in.
data.guard.G39.why.1: Exactly 8 characters and it has a digit, so let it in.
data.guard.G39.why.2: The length is fine but there is no digit, so block it.
data.guard.G39.why.3: It has a digit but only 7 characters, so it is too short. Block it.
data.guard.G39.why.4: It has a digit but is too short, so block it.
data.guard.G39.why.5: It is short and has no digit, so it breaks both rules. Block it.
data.guard.G39.why.6: An empty password is too short from the start, so block it.
data.guard.G4.brief: Guests and Crow are mixed together, all giving passwords. Once 3 wrong tries pile up, block everything after that, even the right password, to stop the endless guessing.
data.guard.G4.concept: Brute force and account lockout (an attacker may lock real users out on purpose, so in practice time-based lockouts and extra checks are used too)
data.guard.G4.crowIntro: Keep knocking and it'll open eventually~
data.guard.G4.crowLose: You only wait for three tries? So impatient!
data.guard.G4.ria: After 3 wrong tries, lock the account. Once locked, block even correct passwords.
data.guard.G4.title: Crow Knocking All Night
data.guard.G4.why.0: A guest gave the right password, so let them in.
data.guard.G4.why.1: A guest's typo. It is wrong, so block it; the wrong count is now 1.
data.guard.G4.why.2: Not locked yet, so the right password gets in.
data.guard.G4.why.4: Wrong try number 3, so the account locks now.
data.guard.G4.why.5: Right after the lock, block even a correct password. Crow may have just guessed it.
data.guard.G40.brief: The farm stats screen sends SQL text to the database. This account must be read-only. Return True only if the query, after stripping spaces at both ends, starts with SELECT (case does not matter) and has no ; at all. No real database is used; the SQL text is only checked as a string.
data.guard.G40.crowIntro: From the read window, maybe I can sneak in some other work~
data.guard.G40.crowLose: A key that only reads? I can't touch anything!
data.guard.G40.ria: The stats screen only needs permission to read. Not being able to write or delete at all is least privilege. Chaining another query with ; must be blocked too. Real least privilege means granting the database account itself only SELECT permission; this text check is one extra layer of safety on top of that.
data.guard.G40.title: A Read-Only Key
data.guard.G40.why.0: A read query that starts with SELECT, so let it in.
data.guard.G40.why.1: After stripping the leading spaces and uppercasing, it starts with SELECT, so let it in.
data.guard.G40.why.2: An aggregate is still a read, so let it in.
data.guard.G40.why.3: Another query is chained after the ;, so block it.
data.guard.G40.why.4: Even the trailing ; is not allowed by this rule, so block it.
data.guard.G40.why.6: It changes data, so block it.
data.guard.G40.why.7: It inserts data, so block it.
data.guard.G40.why.8: An empty query does not start with SELECT, so block it.
data.guard.G40.why.9: Even with SELECT inside, the query starts with DELETE, so it deletes. Check how it starts.
data.guard.G41.brief: The stats screen should only show numeric summaries. Return True only if the uppercased query has no ;, has neither a PHONE column nor an ADDRESS column, has SELECT exactly once, and what it pulls out (between SELECT and FROM) is only COUNT(...) or AVG(...) summaries. No real database is used; the SQL text is only checked as a string.
data.guard.G41.concept: Minimal exposure of personal data (data minimization)
data.guard.G41.crowIntro: Maybe I can slip a phone number in between the summaries~
data.guard.G41.crowLose: Only numbers come out, so there is nothing to steal!
data.guard.G41.ria: Taking out only what the screen needs is data minimization. A count or an average is enough, and columns like phone or address must be left out entirely.
data.guard.G41.title: Numbers Instead of Names
data.guard.G41.why.0: It only counts students, so let it in.
data.guard.G41.why.1: It only takes an average score, so let it in.
data.guard.G41.why.10: Even inside a summary it touches the phone column, so this rule blocks it.
data.guard.G41.why.11: Looking only at the first SELECT, it is just a summary, but a second SELECT after UNION pulls out the names, so block it. SELECT must appear only once.
data.guard.G41.why.2: Even in lowercase, uppercasing gives COUNT( so let it in.
data.guard.G41.why.3: It pulls the name and phone columns as they are, so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.4: Even with an aggregate, it pulls the address column too, so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.5: It pulls names without any aggregate, so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.6: It pulls every column, so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.7: This rule only allows COUNT( and AVG( so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.8: The first part is a summary, but a query that pulls out every name is chained after the ;, so block it.
data.guard.G41.why.9: A tel column is pulled out as it is next to the summary, so block it. This check looks at whether what comes out starts with COUNT( or AVG(. Joining columns together with || is still beyond a check this simple.
data.guard.G42.brief: SQL fragments are mixed into the name field of the seed order form. If it contains any of a single quote ('), a comment mark (--) or a semicolon (;), treat it as a trace of SQL injection and return False; if it has none, return True. Look for the traces with a regular expression.
data.guard.G42.concept: SQL injection (concept) - the real defense is a parameterized query
data.guard.G42.crowIntro: Maybe I'll put just one quote in the name field~
data.guard.G42.crowLose: Quotes, comments and semicolons all get caught!
data.guard.G42.ria: Filtering characters like this is only a stopgap. The real defense is a parameterized query, which sends values separately from the SQL text. Still, it is good to notice suspicious traces early.
data.guard.G42.title: SQL Fragments in the Order Form
data.guard.G42.why.0: A plain name with no traces, so let it in.
data.guard.G42.why.1: Only letters, a digit and a space, so let it in.
data.guard.G42.why.2: Only one hyphen, so it is not a comment mark (--). Let it in.
data.guard.G42.why.3: It has a single quote and a comment mark, so block it.
data.guard.G42.why.4: It has a single quote, so block it.
data.guard.G42.why.5: It has a comment mark (--), so block it.
data.guard.G42.why.6: It has a semicolon, so block it.
data.guard.G42.why.7: A real name, but it has a single quote, so this rule blocks it. That is why the real defense is a parameterized query.
data.guard.G43.brief: The number of requests per minute arrives one by one. Treat the first 3 as the normal baseline and let them all in. After that, take the average of the values let in so far; block a new value if it is more than 2 times the average (exactly 2 times is let in), otherwise let it in and add it to the baseline. Blocked values are never added to the baseline.
data.guard.G43.crowIntro: If I raise it little by little, the average will follow~
data.guard.G43.crowLose: You don't even let the bad values into the average!
data.guard.G43.ria: You can only spot an anomaly if you know what is normal. If blocked values joined the baseline, the attack would pull the average up and the next attack would slip through.
data.guard.G43.title: A Sudden Jump in Traffic
data.guard.G43.why.0: The first 3 are the baseline, so let it in.
data.guard.G43.why.1: The 2nd baseline value, so let it in.
data.guard.G43.why.10: The average is about 13.6, so twice it is about 27.1. It is inside, so let it in and add it to the baseline.
data.guard.G43.why.11: Boundary: the average is 13.5, so twice it is exactly 27, which is not larger, so let it in. Compute the average as a decimal.
data.guard.G43.why.12: The average of everything let in so far is 15, so twice it is 30. 32 is larger, so block it. Use all the values let in, not just the last few.
data.guard.G43.why.2: The 3rd baseline value, so let it in. The average is 10.
data.guard.G43.why.3: Boundary: exactly 2 times the average of 10, which is not more than that, so let it in.
